newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Timor, a legacy of the colonial past.
newsitem.headline: Timor, a legacy of the colonial past.

text.p: Timor, back in the international spotlight on Friday after the Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded its peace prize to two men seeking a peaceful settlement of the long conflict in Indonesian-ruled East Timor, has been a pawn of international rivalries since the late 16th century.
Indonesia invaded mainly Roman Catholic East Timor on December 7, 1975, after civil war erupted on the equatorial island following the withdrawal of Portuguese authorities four months earlier.
Human rights groups said up to one third of the population, or about 200,000 people, died during the invasion and subsequent fighting and famine.
Portugal set up a trading outpost on the eastern half of Timor early in the 16th century, sharing an island rich in prized aromatic sandalwood with the Dutch.

After World War Two, in which Japanese and Australian troops fought pitched battles on East Timor, Portugal rehabilitated its coffee and sandalwood plantations but left the island largely undeveloped. The Dutch ceased to be the colonial power in Indonesia, including West Timor, in 1941 when Japan invaded and an independent Indonesian republic was proclaimed by Sukarno and Hatta on August 17, 1945.

The Portuguese, unlike the Dutch in the rest of the archipelago, returned after World War Two to run East Timor. But when a military coup ended some four decades of right-wing dictatorship in April 1974, the new leftist Portuguese government sought rapid disposal of the remnants of colonial empire.
Its hasty withdrawal from East Timor sparked civil war.
The United Nations has never recognised Indonesia's subsequent annexation of East Timor -- it already ruled West Timor -- and still regards Portugal as the administering power.
Fretilin guerrillas mounted regular attacks on Indonesian troops for years after the invasion but their numbers now are estimated at less than 200 and the attacks have dwindled.
Protests in recent years have taken the form of East Timorese breaking in to foreign embassies in Jakarta and demanding political asylum. About 90 people have so far been granted asylum in Portugal.

But tensions in the region remain high and Indonesian armed forces, who are posted in strength in the territory, have often been accused of human rights violations and of opening fire on residents with little cause. In 1991, about 200 people were killed when troops fired on protesters in the capital Dili.
